summary: This proposed standard specifies the algorithms, parameters, key formats, key sizes and signature formats for subscribers of the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) who sign certificates, certificate revocation lists and other signed objects. Setting one profile helps everyone interoperate. It builds on the broader RPKI specifications.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7935 sets common cryptographic rules for signing and checking RPKI certificates, revocation lists and signed objects. Using one profile lets different participants interpret those signatures consistently.

subtitle: The required signature algorithms, key size and formats for RPKI objects.

tldr.problem: RPKI signers and relying parties need to agree on algorithms and key formats so they can create and verify the same signatures.
tldr.mechanism: The profile specifies RSA PKCS #1 version 1.5 with SHA-256, RSA keys with a 2048-bit modulus and a public exponent of 65,537, and the formats used in certificates and CMS objects.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7935 replaces RFC 6485 and has been updated by RFC 8208 and RFC 8608. The profile anticipates future changes to algorithms and key sizes.

today: RFC 7935 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 6485. It has been updated by RFC 8208 and RFC 8608.

sections.title: Purpose of the RPKI Profile
sections.content:
The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) uses digital signatures on certificates, Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs), CMS signed objects and certification requests. Relying parties use signatures to verify these products.

RFC 7935 specifies the signature and hash algorithms, algorithm parameters, public and private key formats, and signature format for RPKI subscribers. It also directs related RPKI documents that referred to RFC 6485 to use this profile.
sections.plainLanguage: RPKI participants need to use compatible methods when they sign and verify data. This RFC defines the algorithms and formats they use.

sections.title: RSA and SHA-256 Identifiers
sections.content:
The profile uses RSA PKCS #1 version 1.5 for signatures and SHA-256 for hashing. The exception is SHA-1 for generating authority and subject key identifiers. Certificates, CRLs and certification requests identify RSA with SHA-256 using the sha256WithRSAEncryption object identifier.

CMS SignedData identifies the digest and signature separately. The digest fields use SHA-256; new objects use rsaEncryption for the SignerInfo signature algorithm. Verifiers MUST accept either rsaEncryption or sha256WithRSAEncryption in that field for compatibility with RFC 6485 objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile uses one RSA signature method and one main hash method. CMS records the hash and signature choices separately, while other products combine them in one identifier.

sections.title: Key and Signature Formats
sections.content:
RSA key pairs used for signatures MUST have a 2048-bit modulus and public exponent 65,537. The public key is carried in subjectPublicKeyInfo and encoded as an RSAPublicKey. Local policy determines the private-key format.

Certificate signatures follow RFC 4055, and signatures in CMS SignerInfos follow RFC 5652. The profile specifies how the key and signature values are represented so a relying party can decode them consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile fixes the public key size and exponent and gives the format for its public representation. It leaves private-key storage to local policy.

sections.title: Why the Profile Replaced RFC 6485
sections.content:
The main change concerns CMS signed objects. RFC 6485 specified sha256WithRSAEncryption for the SignerInfo signatureAlgorithm field, but existing implementations used rsaEncryption. RFC 7935 follows that existing practice rather than requiring a change to implementations.

The RFC describes this as a change to an identifier, not to the cryptographic algorithm: CMS already carries a separate SHA-256 digest identifier. Relying parties still have to accept the earlier identifier when verifying objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The updated profile changes which identifier new CMS objects use, to match existing implementations. It keeps verification compatible with the identifier required by the earlier profile.

sections.title: Security and Future Algorithm Changes
sections.content:
The RFC introduces no new security threats and refers readers to the security guidance for the related certificate, CRL, request and CMS specifications. It expects that RPKI algorithms and key sizes will need updating over time to maintain cryptographic security.

When the profile changes, RFC 6916 defines the procedures for the transition. The RFC does not specify a date for such a future replacement.
sections.plainLanguage: Cryptographic requirements may need to change as security needs change. A separate RFC describes how RPKI participants can transition to a future profile.
